Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, the trigger pattern is not clinically well matched: 'Authority Commands' is more characteristic of interpersonal violence, military, or coercive-control trauma than pediatric medical trauma. 'Arguments' and 'Known People' are broad but plausible; 'Authority Commands' is the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat items depict a strong pervasive danger schema centered on ambush/attack ('scan for exits,' 'on guard even at home,' 'startle to movement') rather than fear linked to medical crisis, loss, or sudden deterioration in the child. This threat profile is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

vignette:
Mereana had once thought of herself as the kind of person who handled crisis well. At 33, working as a network engineer, she was used to troubleshooting systems under pressure, to staying calm while other people panicked. That certainty changed during the winter her six-year-old son became critically ill. What began as a fever and lethargy escalated quickly into an emergency admission, and within days she was spending long nights under fluorescent hospital lights, watching him attached to monitors, hearing the clipped voices of clinicians discussing tests and procedures she could not bear to understand. The worst moments were the examinations and invasive procedures, when strangers leaned over her child and the room filled with the sounds of equipment, his cry, and her own helpless pleading. Even now, she can name those scenes with painful clarity, as though they happened yesterday rather than months ago.

Since then, certain moments have started to feel dangerous in themselves. Arguments, even ordinary ones, immediately put her on edge, because during the hospitalization any disagreement among staff or between relatives seemed to herald bad news, and she had learned to brace herself when voices sharpened. Related people can have the same effect: a text from her son's father, a call from her ex-husband, or even a family member asking too directly about the boy can send her mind back to the hospital and leave her tense before she has fully registered why. When those reminders hit, Mereana does not experience them as neutral cues; they quickly feel like signs that something awful is about to happen, as if the next message, raised voice, or medical question could mean her son is in danger again. The cue and the threat are almost the same in her mind, so a routine interaction can suddenly carry the cold certainty of an emergency. Medical procedures are especially potent. A routine pediatric appointment, a blood draw, or even the sight of a white coat can make her body react as if the emergency were happening again, because those were the moments when she felt most powerless and most afraid of losing her child. Mereana has come to believe that if something can change in a child's health once, it can change without warning again, and that belief keeps her scanning for danger long before anyone else notices anything amiss.

That vigilance has spread into everyday life. At home, she feels on guard even inside her own house, checking doors twice, listening hard when footsteps approach the bedroom, and sitting up too quickly if there is an unexpected movement nearby. A child darting past her in the hallway or a sudden noise from the kitchen can make her flinch as if she is in immediate danger. Living at that pitch of alertness, Mereana has found that the world seems full of reminders she cannot stop reading for danger. Already feeling threatened, she starts noticing the smallest irregularities - a delayed text, an unfamiliar car idling nearby, a phone vibrating at the wrong time - and each one seems to confirm that something bad could happen without warning. She notices her body first-her heart racing, her stomach dropping, a sharp physical surge that feels embarrassingly out of proportion-but to her it makes sense: if she stays alert enough, she may catch the next emergency before it overwhelms her. Her mind has learned to treat ordinary moments as warning signs. In the quiet of the evening, after her son is asleep, she still finds herself listening for changes in his breathing through the baby monitor she cannot quite stop using, even though he is no longer a baby. When her ex-husband calls to discuss schedules, she hears not just the call but the old possibility of news she cannot control, and the conversation leaves her shaking and keyed up long after it ends.

Over the months, this state of constant alertness has narrowed her world. She has begun avoiding arguments where she can, ending conversations quickly, and keeping interactions with relatives brief so no one asks too many questions about her son's health. At work, she has stayed remote whenever possible, partly because she can control her environment better there, but also because being in shared spaces makes her feel exposed, as though another unexpected movement or sudden complaint could set her body off again. The distance has protected her in some ways, but it has also made her more isolated, and she has noticed that her marriage ended under the strain of all of it. She does not describe the divorce angrily; she describes it as something that happened while she was trying to keep functioning, while everyone else seemed to want answers she could not give.

Mereana came to treatment after realizing that the loop had begun to govern her days. The more she felt on guard, the more she interpreted arguments, familiar voices, and medical settings as signs that danger was close; the more those situations triggered her, the more certain she became that she could never fully relax, even at home. She sought help after a recent pediatric follow-up left her sweating, trembling, and unable to settle for the rest of the day, and after her son asked why she "looked scared all the time." What she wants most is to stop reacting as if every sudden movement or raised voice means catastrophe is about to happen. What frightens her most is that, unless something changes, she will remain trapped in the role of watcher and guard, unable to feel safe with the child she worked so hard to keep alive.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: No paragraph clearly shows triggers/reminders causing a sense of threat; the vignette describes triggers leading to being on edge or re-experiencing the hospital, but not explicitly to perceived danger/threat within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph clearly shows a sense of threat causing triggers/reminders; the vignette describes threat-like hypervigilance and avoidance, but not that feeling threatened generates specific triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
